final.title: Measure email threading before you automate
final.body:
If you are thinking about email threading, treat it as a workflow decision first, not a software feature. The question is not “can a tool sort emails?” It is whether your team keeps losing context because replies drift, follow-ups get split across threads, or the same answer has to be written twice. For a small business, that is the part worth measuring.

Start with one manual check: review one week of email activity and mark every thread that went off track. Note what broke the thread, how long it took to recover the context, and whether the same issue kept repeating. That gives you a plain, visible count of the problem before you ask software to fix it. No need to turn every inbox wobble into a project; the inbox already has enough opinions.

If the pattern is real, the next decision is bounded: improve the setup you already use, or treat AI-assisted categorisation or routing as a narrow pilot candidate. Keep the scope tight. Do not extend it to bulk email, compliance-heavy correspondence, or any step that would need autonomous decisions. Human approval stays in place for anything high-risk.

final.title: Measure email threading before you automate it
final.body:
If email threading is becoming a nuisance, treat it as a workflow decision before you treat it as an AI problem. The real question is not whether the inbox looks neat. It is whether replies are hard to follow, context gets split, or follow-ups keep slipping.

Start with one manual check: review one week of email activity and mark the threads that went off track. For each one, note why it happened and how long it took to recover the context. That gives you a grounded view of whether threading loss is a real recurring cost in your own business, or just inbox friction.

If the problem repeats, the next decision is bounded. First ask whether your current email or CRM setup can be configured better. If not, and the workflow needs a narrow form of categorisation or routing, an AI-assisted pilot may be worth considering. Keep the scope tight. Do not include bulk email, compliance-heavy correspondence, or anything that would require autonomous decisions. Human approval stays in place for the risky bits, which is usually where the trouble starts.
